subject: Factor analysis with likert-scale data and heavy boundries

messages.author: 7d7bd1f061fa8249
messages.subject: Factor analysis with likert-scale data and heavy boundries
parts:
I am doing factor analysis (initially exploratory and then confirmatory) using data from a histology data set with 14 indicator variables that are scaled on a 0 -3 ordered scale of abnormality.  As is often the case with these sorts of histology data, a large fraction (up to 50%) of the values in each variable is 0s (no abnormality).  There are some missing data, as well, but less than 30% for any one variable, and less than 5% for most variables.  I have several questions, but the most important one deals with the heavy loading on 0 values.  My sense is that these data are no more pathological in terms of the short Likert-scale and missing data than most questionnaire type data.  But my references seem to indicate that there is a particular problem with the large load of values on 0s (the lowest value for any variable).

To deal with the issue of non-normality, I plan to use the psych::mixedCor approach to optimize the input correlation/covariance matrices, and the discussion about blavaan has suggested that using the Bayesian approach will ameliorate the issues of non-normality of the indicator variables.  The missing data is essentially all MCAR, and it seems as though this can be managed using 'missing = "ml".'  But what about the heavy 0 loads?  Will this lead to problems?  Is there a "best" way to deal with a heavy load of "boundry" 0s?

Any suggestions will be gratefully received.  Thanks, all, in advance
Larry Hunsicker
Prof (Emeritus) of Medicine
U. Iowa

messages.author: 9b7a59c6f2d552cc
messages.subject: Re: Factor analysis with likert-scale data and heavy boundries
parts:
If you plan to do a log transformation of the variables with many zero values it is conventional to Add a constant value to each value of variable before doing the log transformation. This removes problems with using that transformation on zero. 
Nonetheless, this tradition is not necessarily the way you should go: See https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4120293/ 
Gavin Brown

messages.subject: Re: Factor analysis with likert-scale data and heavy boundries
parts: Nonetheless, this tradition is not necessarily the way you should go: See https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4120293/

Additionally, log-transformation was only ever meant to help make continuous variables look more normal.  We have robust estimators to release that assumption, so transformation is not necessary.

Furthermore, you only have 4 categories, so no monotonic transformation will help.  Your histogram will have a spike at the transformed zeros just like it had for the original zeros.  The more appropriate thing to do would be to treat your data as ordinal, because that's what they are.

Many thanks to Terrence Jorgensen!!  This was exactly the guidance that I was looking for.  At a first glance through the first reference, it seems as though the psych::mixedCor() function does the polychoric correlations that the first paper discusses.  It will take me a day or so to digest all this properly. 
But as I understand things, there is still the assumption that the underlying factors that I am trying to estimate are normally distributed.  This is clearly not correct, as we are looking at degrees of injury, and there can't be less than 0 injury.  There would seem to be theoretical problems with assuming that a latent variable (that may indeed be continuous) is normally distributed when a large fraction of the distribution is at an extreme.    So practically speaking, is there a serious problem with making the assumption of "underlying normality of the latent factor" when it obviously can't be really correct?  I.e., can I profitably take Box's aphorism to heart that "All models are wrong; some are useful."?
Larry Hunsicker

messages.author: 7d7bd1f061fa8249
messages.subject: Re: Factor analysis with likert-scale data and heavy boundries
parts:
Let me be a bit more specific in asking my question.  I am examining a set of 14 variables grading various abnormalities found in a set of biopsies of a specific condition, each scaled on a 0 - 3+ degree of abnormality, with 0 being no abnormality and 3+ being "severe" changes.  A typical distribution of the responses in a set of 380 biopsies is:  0 -196; 1+ - 119; 2+ - 39, 3+ 26.  The asymmetry of the other variables is similar.  Now as I read the Rhemtulla paper, one can do a factor analysis on this data set using polychoric data if one can assume either that the underlying latent variables are normally distributed, or if one can assume that "the model relating the probability of the observed responses y to the values of the latent factors f is a generalized linear model with an ordered probit (or an appropriately scaled logit) link function."  Given that the modal value for "damage" in any of the 14 indicators is 0 (normal, no damage, lower boundry), it is obvious that any underlying latent factor can't be normal.  I read the second condition to assume that the underlying degree of damage along any of the possible latent factor axes can be assumed to predict with consistent probability the damage grade assigned by the pathologist to the indicator variables according to some at least monotonic relationship.  I suppose that this assumption is reasonable in the case of my data set, though there is no way that this could be assessed in practice, since it is precisely that latent damage value that we are trying to assess.  However, later in the paper there is a comment that "Collectively, these studies suggest that continuous and categorical estimation techniques may be robust to mildly asymmetric threshold values but not extremely asymmetric ones."  I have to assume that the distribution that I cite above would have to be called "extremely asymmetric." 
So, to cut to the chase, is it reasonable to perform a factor analysis on this data set, given that the ordered categorical indicator variables are so "extremely asymmetric"?  I am not asking whether one can do the analysis.  I have done it and it converges and seems to make sense.  But, as Hamlet said, 'Seems?  I know not "seems."... These but the trappings and the suits of woe." 
A related question is whether these required assumptions are due to the analytic approach to the computations which, because they are based on normal theory, depend on them.  Are they similarly required when one uses Bayesian analytical methods that basically use MCMC methods to assess correlations and so forth?
Larry Hunsicker

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Factor analysis with likert-scale data and heavy boundries
parts:
there can't be less than 0 injury.  There would seem to be theoretical problems with assuming that a latent variable (that may indeed be continuous) is normally distributed when a large fraction of the distribution is at an extreme ...to cut to the chase, is it reasonable to perform a factor analysis on this data set, given that the ordered categorical indicator variables are so "extremely asymmetric"?

The real issue is not asymmetry of thresholds, but that the assumption of an underlying normal distribution does not fit your data.  Even if it is a discretization of a continuous variable, it would have to have a lower bound of 0, correct?  Then the assumptions underlying the item-factor analysis approach are not met, so no, I would not recommend relying on those assumptions.
Are they similarly required when one uses Bayesian analytical methods that basically use MCMC methods to assess correlations and so forth?

The nice thing about Bayesian modeling programs (e.g., Stan or JAGS) is that they are flexible enough that you can fit whatever model you want, making whatever distributional assumptions you want, within the confines of the program's capabilities.  The Stan community has a great forum to help guide users, just like this forum:

https://discourse.mc-stan.org/

If you search for IRT examples in Stan, you can find syntax examples using logit links, which do not assume an underlying normal distribution for each discrete indicator.  Of course, if IRT works, you need not "go Bayesian"; you could use the mirt package in R.

Good luck,

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Factor analysis with likert-scale data and heavy boundries
parts:
Larry,
It is entirely possible that I am missing something obvious here but, with that caveat, the conclusion that you cannot use CFA seems a little hasty to me.

Your observed data is on an ordinal scale.  An absolute zero point is not definable on an ordinal scale.  You can assign the meaning "no injury" to the lowest category.  However, when you map categories onto numerals, there is no requirement that "no injury" has to map onto the numeral zero.  The meaning attached to the categories is not represented in the statistical model.

We know that there is a one-to-one correspondence of points on a line segment to points on a ray, and likewise from points on a ray to points on a line. So, your conceptual latent variable with a boundary at zero (which could actually be at any finite value and still represent no injury) can be transformed to a latent variable in which no injury is represented by negative infinity.  Remember that in your bounded continuous variable representation, for any non-zero value, there is always a value between that value and zero.  There is no determinate next higher value above zero.

Understood this way, you have a continuous variable, unbounded at either end, that still represents degree of injury with no injury at the lower extreme.  The factor loadings still have the expected interpretation as the amount of change in the item-latent-variable per unit change in the common-factor-latent-variable.  The thresholds still give you a sense of the relative frequency of the ordinal categorical responses.  If the lowest category is the mode, then you would expect these all to have positive values. 

Because "no injury" is the lowest response option, it is still impossible to give a response representing less than zero injury.  It is just that some no-injury responses correspond to negative values of the degree-of-injury latent variable.  These negative values on the latent variable do not represent less-than-none injuries.  They just represent less-than-average injuries.

Am I missing something?

Keith

http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Factor analysis with likert-scale data and heavy boundries
parts:
Am I missing something?

I don't know, maybe I am.  I am sympathetic to the fact that we can monotonically map bounded continuous variables onto partially or unbounded ones (e.g., probabilities to odds to logits), but the probit model doesn't map the observed discrete response onto a (lower) bounded continuous latent variable. It assumes that latent variable is normal (unbounded).  

My advice to pursue a more flexible in Stan/JAGS was also motivated by being able to specify any latent distribution (including an unbounded distribution, but then transform it, and relate that transformation to the observed discrete responses via the threshold model). But that involves quite a bit of savvy.

My concern about using the probit model (standard SEM approach) is mainly the past empirical evidence that when the assumption of underlying normality is violated, the probit model yields biased results, inflated Type I errors, etc.: 
https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1673168

And those results hold even for unbounded nonnormal latent distributions.  Given the OP's description, I doubt that the latent variable interpretation is even appropriate.  It seems that biopsy results are either abnormal or not (majority not, so zero-inflated), and among the abnormal, there are varying degrees of abnormality that could arguably have been reduced to a few nonzero categories.  In which case, maybe a hurdle model would be more appropriate.

But I could be misreading the situation.  The case of "lack of abnormality" might not correspond to an absolute zero.  Instead, there might be a lot of (latent) variability among the cases considered normal.  Still no idea whether the latent distribution could reasonably be expected to approximate normality, but I don't know enough about how these indicators were "scaled" in practice to draw any firm conclusion about an absolute zero in the latent distribution.  Thanks for keeping me honest, Keith :-)  

So Lawrence, can you offer any more information about how your 0-3 categories were operationally defined to better inform any advice we might offer?

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 7d7bd1f061fa8249

parts:
Keith:

MANY THANKS!!  You made this all much clearer to me.  First of all, and in response to Terrence as well, there is in my mind a clear (set of) continuous latent variable(s), and, inspired by Keith's comments, a clear way for me to represent it.  Let me start by being less cagey about the data.  I am looking at data from a batch of "index" transplant kidney biopsies from patients with onset of new kidney graft dysfunction at varying periods following transplantation.  These biopsies are graded on 14 Likert scales from 0 - 3+ for findings thought to represent various consequences of different types of transplant immune injury -- presence of donor specific antibody (of two classes), complement activation, microvascular inflammation, and cell mediated immune injury, and simple scarring, with a possible but controversial fifth type of injury -- ongoing inflammation and tubular injury in areas of scarring.  These have all been graded in accordance with the "Banff" grading scheme, which was developed and has been highly refined more to achieve and permit agreement in scoring (a big issue in Pathology where there remains a large fraction of "individual judgment") than to correlate the injury seen on the slides with the adverse clinical impact on kidney function or graft survival.  Our motivation for undertaking factor analysis is to reduce the complexity of 14 different grading scales to identify differentiable types of injury (factors) so as to facilitate understanding which forms of injury or scarring are important leading to the outcomes of the newly developed graft dysfunction. 

So...  The appropriate infinite and continuous latent variables can be understood as log transformed degrees of underlying injury -- not of the Likert score which would be inappropriate -- along one axis of injury.  As Keith has pointed out, zero injury can be represented as negative infinity -- the log of 0.  Though the Banff grading scheme discretizes the amount of injury, the injury is clearly not itself discrete -- at least on any recognizable granularity.  There may be injury present that is not identifiable (graded 0) because it is so minor.  Indeed, the first cut point -- between 0 and 1 on the Likert scale corresponds to something well recognized in Lab Medicine, that there is a minimum detectable level of something -- whether it is chemical species or an amount of injury seen on a slide.  Clearly as injury develops in a transplanted kidney there isn't a sudden jump between a pristine biopsy and one that is now finally identifiable as exhibiting injury.  Further, use of a log transform of the (latent) injury is justified by the widely recognized psychological phenomenon that we tend to grade things on a log-linear scale -- whether it is brightness or loudness or the degree of injury on a slide.  So a 2 on the Banff Likert scale doesn't mean twice the amount of injury seen in a "just discernably abnormal" amount of injury; it means a "substantial" amount of injury.  And a score of 3 means "really serious injury."  And there is no requirement that the modal value in any of the 14 scales has to be 0.  One of the measures of scarring is mostly scored as 1+.  A set of really bad biopsies might all be scored as 3+.  So while the distributions of Likert scores of most of the 14 indicator variables look more like a Poisson than a normal distribution, there is no inherent reason that they have to be that way.  It is just that we chose to look at biopsies at the first significant point that cliinical injury could be identified. 

Now the question, it seems to me, is whether one has to worry that the Likert scores have a heavy boundary score (0), or that the scores represent cuts along a log-linear rather than a linear scale.  My intuition is that, since log transform is order preserving, it doesn't make any difference to the calculations of the covariances/correlations as calculated using the mxedCor approach.  And as I have read further in the Rhemtulla paper, that seems to be their recommendation based on a 4 value Likert scale and probable non-normality (skew) of the values.  This now seems to me to be a reasonable approach. 

But, as I quoted before, 'Seems?  I know not "seems."'  I' not a bad physician or clinical investigator.  But I am really pushing the edge of my understanding of factor analysis. Does this approach now seem reasonable to those of you with a better understanding of this?  (And I do have a bias that Bayesian MCMC does better with non-normal distributions than a purely analytical approach.  Is this reasonable?)

Thanks to both of you for leading my brain in what I hope has been an appropriate direction.

Larry Hunsicker

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Factor analysis with likert-scale data and heavy boundries
parts:
The appropriate infinite and continuous latent variables can be understood as log transformed degrees of underlying injury ...  As Keith has pointed out, zero injury can be represented as negative infinity -- the log of 0. 

Okay, but that understanding is entirely in your head.  The software's algorithm has no such understanding.  If you assume the Likert scale is a polytomized realization of a log-transformed common factor with a lower bound of zero (transformed to -Inf), then you are estimating parameters in that context and drawing inferences about polychoric correlations among what you assert to be log-transformed latent variables.  As long as your are comfortable defending that approach, I'm not saying it is wrong.  

But perhaps this numerical example explains better what I am warning about.  The common and unique factors above all have SD == 1, and factor loadings are 1 (intercepts are 0, omitted), so the commonality is comparable across the normal and zero-bound/skewed case.

set.seed(123)
## draw latent factor
Normal <- rnorm(380)
Skewed <- rchisq(380, df = 1) # SD == 1 because sqrt(df) == 1
## draw 3 residuals to make 3 items for each
n1 <- Normal + rnorm(380)
n2 <- Normal + rnorm(380)
n3 <- Normal + rnorm(380)
s1 <- Skewed + rchisq(380, df = 1)
s2 <- Skewed + rchisq(380, df = 1)
s3 <- Skewed + rchisq(380, df = 1)
dataN <- data.frame(n1, n2, n3)
dataS <- data.frame(s1, s2, s3)

## estimate correlation in each scenario
cor(dataN)
cor(dataS) # similar to correlations among normal variables
cor(data.frame(lapply(dataS, log))) # correlations among log-transformed variables are lower

All statistical methods are based on assumptions, some on more/stronger ones than others.  The latent-common-factor assumption is already a strong one, and its distributional assumption is arguably also quite strong.  Your analysis just has an extra layer that is even more difficult to test against your data.  Notice that your common factors are more strongly correlated than your log-transformations are.  The implication of a log-transformed common factor further implies that the estimated polychorics (to which your model is fitted) may be quite attenuated.

Good luck,

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Hi, again, Terrance:

Yes.  I get your point.  The first step in either exploratory or confirmatory factor analysis is generation of the correlation/covariance matrix, and it is important to get strength of those correlations as strong and accurate (as free of error) as possible.  If one is doing this based on normal theory  -- Pearson correlation -- (whether the underlying variables are normal or not) one would want the correlations to be based on the actual numbers themselves, and not on some transform of them.  In your example, one would expect a 50% covariance between any two of the vectors since half of the value of each member of the vector pairs is the same value.   This assumption falls apart when one is comparing the logs of the underlying values.  Even so, I am surprised that the Pearson correlation is degraded so little when applied to the log transforms.  For what it's worth, your Chi square variable example looks on histogram a good bit like my data -- clearly left truncated at 0 and with a mode at the lowest level.  So evidently the correlations don't worry too much about the normality of the data. 
But I am dealing with ordered factors where the only assumption is that order is more or less preserved.  When one repeats your demonstration using Kendall rather than Pearson correrlation, there is no difference between the estimated correlations of the untransformed variables and the log transformed variables.  

> cor(dataN, method = 'kendall')
          n1        n2        n3
n1 1.0000000 0.3317317 0.3238161
n2 0.3317317 1.0000000 0.3465630
n3 0.3238161 0.3465630 1.0000000
> cor(dataS, method = 'kendall') 
          s1        s2        s3
s1 1.0000000 0.3081516 0.3049299
s2 0.3081516 1.0000000 0.3601444
s3 0.3049299 0.3601444 1.0000000
> cor(data.frame(lapply(dataS, log)), method = 'kendall') 
          s1        s2        s3
s1 1.0000000 0.3081516 0.3049299
s2 0.3081516 1.0000000 0.3601444
s3 0.3049299 0.3601444 1.0000000

The Kendall correlations in the first two calls above are reduced by about 40% (~50% to 30%) compared with the Pearson correlations in your example.  But the Kendall correlations between the values themselves and the log transform are identical (2nd and 3rd calls), because the log transform is order preserving. 

Further, my data are ordered factors.  Even the order is only preserved approximately.  All the values within one level of the ordered factor are considered to be the same.  This is the reality of my data.  On any of the indicator variable scales, I can only reasonably say that the "damage" in one biopsy is probably greater than in another one when this somewhat arbitrary "score" is higher.  The Rhemtulla paper that you pointed out to me suggests that I should be using a still different way to compute my underlyng correlation matrix -- cat-LS methods -- because the number of levels is < 5 and the data are likely to be quite non-normal.  Fortunately my N (about 380 biopsies) is pretty good.

So, yes, I am comfortable in my head that a log transformed (or now, for that matter, even a left truncated at 0 non-transformed) scale is a reasonable model of the underlying latent variable, and it seems to me that if I use the appropriate order preserving correlation coefficients, I won't lose any more power than I lose in reality by the fact that only the order, not the actual value, of the variable means anything. 

I still have two questions.  Rhemtulla suggests that I should be using polychoric correlations and cat-LS robust variances to calculate my correlation matrix,.  What is/are the correct R function(s) to do this?  There is psych::mixedCor and lavaan::lavCor that seem to be doing this with polychoric correlations.  Robust variances??

I am biased to use MCMC type calculations when I am unsure that my data are anywhere close to "normal theory."  Blavaan is available and only costs enough time for me to get a cup of tea.  Should I be using blavaan rather than straight forward lavaan?

Larry

On Monday, November 25, 2019 at 9:57:17 AM UTC-6, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
The appropriate infinite and continuous latent variables can be understood as log transformed degrees of underlying injury ...  As Keith has pointed out, zero injury can be represented as negative infinity -- the log of 0. 

Okay, but that understanding is entirely in your head.  The software's algorithm has no such understanding.  If you assume the Likert scale is a polytomized realization of a log-transformed common factor with a lower bound of zero (transformed to -Inf), then you are estimating parameters in that context and drawing inferences about polychoric correlations among what you assert to be log-transformed latent variables.  As long as your are comfortable defending that approach, I'm not saying it is wrong.  

But perhaps this numerical example explains better what I am warning about.  The common and unique factors above all have SD == 1, and factor loadings are 1 (intercepts are 0, omitted), so the commonality is comparable across the normal and zero-bound/skewed case.

set.seed(123)
## draw latent factor
Normal <- rnorm(380)
Skewed <- rchisq(380, df = 1) # SD == 1 because sqrt(df) == 1
## draw 3 residuals to make 3 items for each
n1 <- Normal + rnorm(380)
n2 <- Normal + rnorm(380)
n3 <- Normal + rnorm(380)
s1 <- Skewed + rchisq(380, df = 1)
s2 <- Skewed + rchisq(380, df = 1)
s3 <- Skewed + rchisq(380, df = 1)
dataN <- data.frame(n1, n2, n3)
dataS <- data.frame(s1, s2, s3)

## estimate correlation in each scenario
cor(dataN)
cor(dataS) # similar to correlations among normal variables
cor(data.frame(lapply(dataS, log))) # correlations among log-transformed variables are lower

All statistical methods are based on assumptions, some on more/stronger ones than others.  The latent-common-factor assumption is already a strong one, and its distributional assumption is arguably also quite strong.  Your analysis just has an extra layer that is even more difficult to test against your data.  Notice that your common factors are more strongly correlated than your log-transformations are.  The implication of a log-transformed common factor further implies that the estimated polychorics (to which your model is fitted) may be quite attenuated. 

Good luck,

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Factor analysis with likert-scale data and heavy boundries
parts: Rhemtulla suggests that I should be using polychoric correlations and cat-LS robust variances to calculate my correlation matrix,.  What is/are the correct R function(s) to do this?  There is psych::mixedCor and lavaan::lavCor that seem to be doing this with polychoric correlations.  Robust variances??

That is already what lavaan does.  DWLS estimation involves first estimating thresholds from observed proportions univariate tables, then polychoric correlations based on those (and polyserial correlations between ordered and continuous outcomes).  Then the model is fitted to reproduce those thresholds and polychorics.  The vcov() is already robust.
Should I be using blavaan

blavaan uses Stan (or optionally JAGS) under the hood, and makes the same assumptions about the data being normal.  It does not yet handle categorical outcomes, so if you are interested in this route, you should just jump straight to looking for IRT (graded response model) examples in Stan.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

When we said that 2 variables/factors are correlated, we are saying that we expect the 2 variables to be multivariate normal. These are saying the same. Since SEM use the covariance matrix as input, assumes that the data and factors are multivariate normal.

In practice, Bayesian SEM behaves similar to a robust method like MLR. But it is still part of the model. For models that directly account for non-normality, you would have to code the model to use another distribution instead of nroaml, like t, of skew for example. But would required more work as there is no automated program for this

For EFA with polychoric correlation, you can use the ?semTools::efaUnrotate function from semTools. It ateks lavaan arguments, such as ordered and estimator to do the EFA with DWLS for example.

parts:
Now I'm really confused.  A look at Terrence Jorgensen's posting two above shows clearly that three grossly non-normal vectors (his middle model of three "Skewed" vectors -- actually skewed and lower-bounded at 0)  can be correlated.  No assumption of normality or even unboundedness is needed.   Further, their degree of correlation is indistinguishable from that of the correlation of the three normal distributions (top model).   And if the vectors aren't univariate normal, I'm not sure how they can be multivariate normal.  Further, if ultimately everything in the factor analysis method depends on the correlation/covariance matrix, and the matrices of correlations of normal and skewed vectors can't be distinguished, how can the normality/non-normality of the vectors have any impact on the calculations?  Are you saying that the mechanics of the computations work fine, but that the conclusions are invalid because the underlying assumptions are not met?

Along this same line, the Wirth paper that Terrence referred to me above, dealing with categorical confirmatory factor analysis (CCFA) states that, "CCFA assumes that ordered-categorical item responses are discrete representations of continuous latent responses."  He footnotes that comment with the further note that, "Although the continuous latent response distribution is generally assumed to be normally distributed, it is important to note that this assumption is required only in the presence of correlated unique factors; otherwise, the assumption is one of statistical convenience (i.e., it reduces complexities associated with estimation; see Pearson, 1900).  Though I didn't find any explicit discussion about whether the latent factor might be left-truncated at 0, his discussion of the threshold parameters doesn't seem to require that there be any distributional mass below 0, so long as there was some below the lowest threshold -- presumably to permit the estimation of the underlying multivariate distribution.  I can see how the assumption of multivariate normality can make the multivariate distributional computations easier.  But is it theoretically required?

I'm still working my way through Wirth.  But it seems to me that what I am trying to do is categorical factor analysis (both exploratory and confirmatory), and maybe I ought to be  using methods that were designed for that type of model.

Larry Hunsicker

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Factor analysis with likert-scale data and heavy boundries
parts:
Larry,
  This comes with two caveats.  General caveat:  I spend my time thinking about the semantics of SEM, not estimation.  Specific caveat:  I have not yet obtained a copy of the Foldnes & Grønneberg (2019) article although I have read the piece by Maydeu-Olivares et al. (2009) which it cites.

  Just to be clear, my previous post was not intended to discourage you from exploring Baysian methods.

  I think that you are fine mixing variables treated as ordinal and as continuous.

  Robust standard errors can handle things like skewness.

  If you just had one ordinal variable, unless I am missing something, there would be no possible distribution of values that could not be be reproduced by categorizing a normal random variate.  The assumption of normality is just an identifying assumption with no empirical content in this case.

  The constraints come with two or more variables in requiring not just univariate normal distributions but also linear associations between the variables.  So, the thought experiment is whether or not it seems plausible to assume linear associations between the normally distributed representations of the latent variables.

  If you sum two normally distributed variables with a non-linear association, you can obtain a non-normally distributed result.  This violates multivariate normality because it requires that every linear combination of variables be normally distributed.

  At a more conceptual level, covariance is a measure of linear association.  If one or more pairs of variables bears a non-linear association, then the covariance matrix cannot adequately represent the joint probability distribution of the variables.  Unless I have misunderstood something, tests of multivariate normality actually test this consequence of multivariate normality, providing an indirect test of multivariate normality itself.

  Terrence's example very nicely illustrated a case in which the log transform produces a lower correlation.  The opposite is also possible (see below script).  I believe that this primarily depends upon which representation produces linear associations between the variables.  Normalizing transformations often have the side effect of changing the shape of the associations between variables.  The association could be linear before after a given transformation.  Measures of linear association will only capture part of a non-linear association.

nObs <- 10000
LNormalX <- log(rnorm(nObs,10,2))
errorSD <- sqrt( (sd(LNormalX)^2) * 2)
LNormalY <- LNormalX + rnorm(nObs,0,errorSD) #linear association
ExpX <- exp(LNormalX) #normally distributed
ExpY <- exp(LNormalY)

cor(LNormalX, LNormalY)
cor(log(ExpX), log(ExpY)) #larger value
cor(ExpX, ExpY)           #smaller value

  Of course, we often accept linear approximations as reasonable even when strict linearity is not plausible.  Practical significance has a role to play in deciding how much is too much.

Hope that helps,

Keith

parts: OK.  Now I am beginning to think that I understand where the need for the multivariate assumption comes from.  (I may be a bit closer to thinking "It is..." than "It seems...")

If you just had one ordinal variable, unless I am missing something, there would be no possible distribution of values that could not be be reproduced by categorizing a normal random variate.  The assumption of normality is just an identifying assumption with no empirical content in this case.

"Unless I am missing something..."  the Foldnes paper says exactly that.  You just take an arbitrary normal distribution and chop it into pieces that have the same distributional mass as in the empirical levels of the ordinal "indicator" variable.  You can do this with each of the Likert type variables.  The problem arises when you want to estimate correlations among all these arbitrarily chosen normal distributions with totally empirical cut-points.  As Foldnes points out, the data may not permit identification of a specific fit.  There may be many multivariate normal models that would fit the existing data.  The estimation of the correlations of paired values from each of the pairs of variables looks at the empiric X by X contingency tables and fits a multivariate normal distribution to them.  But that is what assumes that each of the fit variable vectors has a linear relationship to each of the others.   There is no mathematical reason to assume that we will have chosen the correct model -- that the next sampling of the "real world" somewhere else along the axes of the assumed multivariate space will be reasonably approximately fit by the same multivariate distribution. 

That, it seems to me, is where my mental model comes in.  I am assuming that our evaluation of the amount of damage along any of the 14 axes of the Banff scale is likely to be roughly logarhithmic -- not because the distribution of damage is necessarily going to be logarhthmic, but because of our psychology that is likely to chop our estimates of damage at roughly logarithmic cut points.  So in my case, the argument for assuming a roughly multivariate normal distribution of the assumed latent factors reflects not the reality of the distribution of injury in the biopsy, but instead the reality of our psychology in seeing and classifying damage in roughly logarhithmic degrees of severity.

Again, "Unless I am missing something," this implies that tests of the assumed multivariate normality require us to check not just the fit of the model to the current data -- the model that was just fit to the current data -- but also to data sets located elsewhere in the hypothesized model space than at the metacenter of the current data. 

In any case, I have managed to become comfortable in using (as a model) the polychoric methods of lavaan.  This comfort is made greater by the fact that my first exploratory FA makes total sense.  That is, the model that I fit to my data looks pretty much like I sort of thought it should before I fit the model -- surprise, surprise.  But I do have a completely separate data set to try it on once I figure out how to complete this first one correctly.  That should be a more convincing test.

Once more, thanks to all for helping me think all this through!

Larry Hunsicker
